:chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}[Download the corrected Card Weather CSV](sandbox:/mnt/data/data-10_corrected.csv)

content.text:
This is every on entry card

[User attached 1 file; file contents were not included]

items.text:
Exactly — and this is a strong validation of the canonicalization. Your list contains **59 cards**, and the refined corpus contained exactly **59 occurrences of `entry`**. So at least for this trigger, the text itself is already functioning as reliable metadata.

I would therefore **not manually mark these 59 cards**. During simulator compilation, scan each tokenized description for:

```text
[on] [entry]
```

and set the card's trigger bit automatically:

\[
\text{triggerMask}[card]\;|\!=\;\text{ON\_ENTRY}
\]

Then parse only what follows that trigger until the next clause/trigger boundary. For example:

```text
on entry | attack enemy 3 x damage ; gain 10 % stats each turn
^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
trigger          entry effect
```

The `each turn` clause becomes a separate registered ability.

This gives you a useful two-stage representation:

```text
compile time:
description tokens
→ detect triggers
→ build event handlers

runtime:
ON_ENTRY event
→ look up only this card's compiled ON_ENTRY handlers
→ execute effects
```

So the simulator never searches all 59 cards when an entry happens. The **description search happens once during compilation**. After that, a card might store something compact like:

```text
trigger bits:
00000101...

ON_ENTRY handler range:
effects[37:40]
```

or simply an index into its ability list.

And the fact that `entry` appears once per card is particularly nice: your 59-name list gives us an immediate test condition:

\[
\boxed{\#\text{cards detected by `[on,entry]`} = 59}
\]

If the compiler returns 58 or 60, we know either the canonical corpus or parser is wrong.

This is probably how I'd build the simulator generally: **canonical phrases generate the metadata automatically**, rather than maintaining separate hand-written lists of cards for each primitive.

content.text: but I can search for on entry to get all the cards it applies to no?

items.text:
Yes — exactly. That’s the big advantage of the canonical descriptions.

If every entry-triggered ability is normalized to the literal token sequence:

```text
on entry
```

then you can scan the corpus once, find every card containing that pattern, and automatically assign the `ON_ENTRY` trigger to those cards.

You can do the same for many other primitives:

```text
on death
each turn
after attacking
when attacked
below 25 % HP
chance to
revive
freeze
poison
steal
```

So instead of manually attaching every primitive to every card, you can build **pattern-to-primitive compilation rules**.

For example:

```text
"on entry"      -> trigger = ON_ENTRY
"on death"      -> trigger = ON_DEATH
"each turn"     -> trigger = TURN_START
"after attacking" -> trigger = AFTER_ATTACK
```

Then parse the rest of the sentence for the effect.

So:

```text
on entry deal 2 x damage
```

can compile automatically into:

```text
trigger = ON_ENTRY
effect = ATTACK
multiplier = 2
```

and:

```text
on death heal next ally 50 % HP
```

into:

```text
trigger = ON_DEATH
effect = HEAL
target = NEXT_ALLY
amount = 0.5 HP
```

This is also why the canonicalization work matters so much. If you leave:

```text
upon entering battle
when this card enters
on entering
on entry
```

as four variants, your parser has to support four patterns. If you collapse them all to:

```text
on entry
```

the simulator compiler becomes much simpler.

You can think of it as building a small grammar:

\[
\text{trigger} + \text{effect} + \text{target} + \text{magnitude} + \text{condition}.
\]

Then most cards can be compiled from text automatically.

The rare weird cards become the exception list, not the norm.

So yes — rather than “attach primitives individually,” I’d do:

\[
\boxed{\text{search canonical phrases} \rightarrow \text{auto-assign primitives}}
\]

and only manually patch cards whose semantics are too unusual for the grammar.

content.text: You still have to attach the primitive functions to each card individually

items.text:
Yes. That part doesn’t go away.

The abstraction only prevents you from writing **new simulator logic** for every card. You still need a per-card definition that says which primitives that card uses, with what parameters and triggers.

So instead of writing:

```python
if card_id == 173:
    ...
elif card_id == 174:
    ...
```

you’d have data like:

```python
card_173 = [
    Ability(
        trigger=ON_ENTRY,
        effects=[Attack(multiplier=2.0)]
    ),
    Ability(
        trigger=ON_DEATH,
        effects=[Heal(target=NEXT_ALLY, amount=0.5)]
    )
]
```

and another card might be:

```python
card_174 = [
    Ability(
        trigger=TURN_START,
        effects=[
            Conditional(
                condition=HP_BELOW(0.25),
                effect=ModifyIncomingDamage(multiplier=0.5)
            )
        ]
    )
]
```

So yes, **289 cards still means 289 card definitions**.

The win is that each definition becomes mostly declarative assembly rather than bespoke code.

The real question is therefore how much of that attachment can be automated.

Given how canonicalized your descriptions are becoming, you could eventually make the descriptions themselves close enough to a DSL that a parser converts:

```text
on entry deal 2 x damage
```

into:

```text
ON_ENTRY
ATTACK SELF_TARGET=ENEMY MULT=2
```

and:

```text
50 % chance to revive with 1 / 2 HP
```

into:

```text
ON_DEATH
CHANCE 0.5
REVIVE SELF HP_RATIO=0.5
```

Then most cards wouldn’t need manually attached primitives at all. The description parser would generate them.

You’d still manually handle the genuinely unusual cards, especially ones like:

```text
when Piccolo uses its ability to swap with this card...
```

or:

```text
gain an ability based on the card's art
```

But if the canonical descriptions are deliberately engineered around your primitive vocabulary, I think you could make **the majority of cards compile automatically from text**.

That would make the pipeline:

\[
\text{canonical description}
\rightarrow
\text{rule parser}
\rightarrow
\text{primitive list}
\rightarrow
\text{simulator}
\]

while independently:

\[
\text{same canonical description}
\rightarrow
\text{small transformer}
\rightarrow
\text{card embedding}.
\]

That has a nice side effect: the simulator and the language model are both reading the **same source of truth**.

So I’d probably design the canonical language with this in mind. Not just “easy for the transformer to learn,” but also “easy for a deterministic parser to compile.”

content.text: I need to build the simulator first, I was going to start with the first card and incrementally add more features but since you’ve seen them all at once how should it be programmed?

items.text:
Starting from the first card and adding special cases would work initially, but the full set shows that it would eventually become a giant nest of exceptions. The right abstraction is: **cards do not contain code; cards contain small programs made from simulator primitives**.

The simulator itself should know nothing about particular cards such as Piccolo. It should know concepts such as `DAMAGE`, `MODIFY_STAT`, `ON_ENTRY`, `ON_LETHAL`, `SWAP`, `REVIVE`, `COPY_ABILITY`, `DELAY`, `RANDOM_CHOICE`, and `TARGET_CLASS`. The card database then composes those concepts.

For example, this description:

```text
on entry attack with 3 x damage;
gain 10 % stats and damage reduction each turn
```

could compile to approximately:

```text
Ability(
    trigger = ON_ENTRY,
    effects = [
        Attack(target=ACTIVE_ENEMY, multiplier=3)
    ]
)

Ability(
    trigger = TURN_START,
    effects = [
        ModifyStat(SELF, ALL_STATS, +10%),
        ModifyStat(SELF, DAMAGE_REDUCTION, +10%)
    ]
)
```

while

```text
50 % chance to revive with half HP
```

becomes:

```text
Ability(
    trigger = ON_DEATH,
    effects = [
        Chance(
            p=0.50,
            success=Revive(SELF, hp=0.50 * MAX_HP)
        )
    ]
)
```

The crucial thing is that `Chance` can later either sample normally **or branch the probability tree**, without changing the card definition.

### I would build the engine around events

Don't make a turn function that directly performs everything. An attack should generate events:

\[
\text{ATTACK\_DECLARE}
\rightarrow
\text{BEFORE\_HIT}
\rightarrow
\text{DAMAGE\_CALCULATE}
\rightarrow
\text{DAMAGE\_APPLY}
\rightarrow
\text{AFTER\_DAMAGE}
\rightarrow
\text{LETHAL}
\rightarrow
\text{DEATH}
\rightarrow
\text{AFTER\_ATTACK}.
\]

This matters enormously for your cards.

Consider these effects from the dataset:

```text
block first attack
dodge first lethal hit
survive lethal attack with 1 HP
if this card would die, the enemy dies instead
attacker takes damage
counterattack when damaged
on death ...
after attacking ...
```

Those are not seven unrelated mechanics. They're handlers attached to different points in the same event pipeline.

The hardest part is **lethal resolution**, so I would explicitly distinguish:

```text
DAMAGE_APPLIED
    ↓
WOULD_DIE
    ↓
LETHAL_REPLACEMENT
    ↓
DEATH
    ↓
ON_DEATH
```

Then:

```text
survive lethal with 1 HP
```

registers at `LETHAL_REPLACEMENT`.

```text
dodge lethal and switch with ally
```

also registers there.

```text
on death gain 3 fossils
```

registers at `ON_DEATH`.

That prevents extremely nasty ordering bugs later.

### The state should be completely explicit

Your game state should contain everything needed to resume simulation from that exact point:

```text
GameState
    teams
    active card indices
    ordered decks
    card instances
    HP / current stats
    statuses
    temporary modifiers
    permanent modifiers
    counters
    turn number
    extra/skip turns
    delayed events
    field effects
    fossil / void / other resources
    dead cards
    summoned cards
    copied/stolen abilities
```

A **CardDefinition** is immutable:

```text
CardDefinition
    base stats
    classes
    pack
    abilities
    specific relationships
```

while **CardInstance** is mutable:

```text
CardInstance
    definition_id
    current_hp
    current_atk
    modifiers
    statuses
    per-battle counters
    per-card flags
```

That distinction will save you repeatedly. A card can die, revive, transform, steal abilities, gain permanent battle stats, lose ATK, etc., without modifying its underlying definition.

### Most of the 289 cards reduce to a fairly small primitive vocabulary

I would make the effect layer roughly like this:

| Primitive | Covers examples such as |
|---|---|
| `Damage` | normal attacks, entry attacks, Max-HP damage |
| `Heal` | lifesteal, turn healing, full heal |
| `ModifyStat` | +ATK, -damage, stat stealing |
| `ApplyStatus` | freeze, poison, bleed, confusion, slow |
| `RemoveStatus` | immunity/cleansing |
| `ModifyDamage` | halve, 1.5×, caps, reductions |
| `Dodge/Block/Shield` | evade and prevention mechanics |
| `ExtraTurn/SkipTurn` | turn manipulation |
| `Revive` | self/ally resurrection |
| `Kill` | executes and instant death |
| `Swap` | lineup/deck changes |
| `Summon` | copies, Frankenstein, Joy/Sorrow |
| `Transform` | awakened/different-card states |
| `CopyAbility` | fallen ally abilities |
| `StealAbility` | enemy ability theft |
| `DisableAbility` | cancellation/negation |
| `Redirect` | ally damage redirection |
| `Counterattack` | reactive attacks |
| `MoveCard` | front/back/end of deck |
| `DelayedEffect` | “after 5 moves”, “dies in N turns” |
| `FieldEffect` | affects entire team while present |
| `RandomChoice` | random ability/card/target |
| `Repeat` | attack N times |
| `Conditional` | HP threshold, class, rarity, position |
| `Resource` | Fossils, Void stacks, etc. |

The important point is that **multihit should not be its own combat system**. It is just:

```text
Repeat(
    count=3,
    effect=Attack(multiplier=0.5)
)
```

Likewise:

```text
deal 0.5 x, 1 x, then 2 x damage
```

is:

```text
Sequence([
    Attack(0.5),
    Attack(1.0),
    Attack(2.0)
])
```

and:

```text
below 25 % HP, damage taken is halved
```

is:

```text
Conditional(
    condition=HP_RATIO(SELF) <= 0.25,
    effect=ModifyIncomingDamage(multiplier=0.5)
)
```

That compositionality is the key.

### Conditions should also be data

I'd avoid coding separate `if` statements for every card. Have a condition tree:

```text
HP_BELOW(target, value)
HP_ABOVE(target, value)
CLASS_IS(target, class)
CARD_IS(target, card_id)
ALLY_DEAD(count)
HAS_STATUS(target, status)
TURN_MODULO(n)
POSITION_IS(...)
RESOURCE_AT_LEAST(...)
RARITY_COMPARE(...)
```

and combinators:

```text
AND
OR
NOT
```

Then a rare Piccolo-specific interaction doesn't require a huge card bitmap. It can simply contain:

```text
condition =
    CARD_IS(source_of_swap, PICCOLO_ID)
```

That's one sparse card ID in one ability definition.

### Put probability into the engine from day one

This is the part I would **not postpone**, because adding it afterward would infect almost every primitive.

Instead of an effect returning one state:

\[
S\rightarrow S',
\]

let its conceptual interface return:

\[
S\rightarrow
\{(S_1,p_1),(S_2,p_2),\ldots\}.
\]

Deterministic effects simply return:

\[
\{(S',1)\}.
\]

A 50% chance returns:

\[
\{(S_{\text{success}},0.5),
(S_{\text{failure}},0.5)\}.
\]

Two simultaneous independent 50% events naturally produce four branches.

You can still have a fast **sample mode**:

```text
ResolutionMode.SAMPLE
```

and an exhaustive mode:

```text
ResolutionMode.BRANCH
```

using exactly the same card definitions.

That is extremely valuable because you can use sampling while debugging and probability propagation when producing training labels.

Your branch object should be roughly:

```text
Branch
    GameState state
    float probability
```

and after every stochastic resolution:

```text
merge identical states
→ discard/approximate tiny probability branches
→ continue highest-probability unresolved branches
```

A canonical state hash then allows:

\[
(S,p_1)+(S,p_2)
\rightarrow
(S,p_1+p_2).
\]

That could save huge amounts of computation.

### Continuous random effects should compile into intervals

For something like:

```text
gain 1-50 % damage
```

don't make `ModifyStat` understand continuous probability.

Have:

```text
RandomRange(0.01, 0.50)
```

produce intervals whose resulting states differ.

The rest of the engine still receives an ordinary:

```text
ModifyStat(DAMAGE, +x)
```

effect.

So stochasticity stays orthogonal to mechanics.

### Trigger ordering should be explicitly specified

I would establish the precedence rules before implementing many cards. Something approximately like:

```text
turn start
→ delayed effects
→ pre-action statuses
→ choose action
→ declare attack
→ interception / swapping
→ dodge / block
→ outgoing modifiers
→ incoming modifiers
→ shields
→ apply damage
→ reactive effects
→ lethal replacements
→ death
→ death triggers
→ replacement card enters
→ entry triggers
→ after-attack effects
→ turn end
```

You will almost certainly adjust that based on the game's actual rules, but **write the ordering into the engine**, rather than letting whichever ability happens to run first decide it.

When two effects genuinely happen simultaneously, collect them first and resolve them according to a stable priority rule. That also makes your probability branching reproducible.

### Start implementation with primitives, not Card #1

You can still build incrementally, but I would change what "incrementally" means.

Build enough to express a tiny collection like:

```text
vanilla attack
+ stat modifier
+ on-entry trigger
+ chance
+ dodge/block
+ death
```

Then immediately encode every card that can be expressed with those primitives.

When you hit the first unrepresentable card, add **one reusable primitive**, and again encode every newly supported card.

The progression therefore becomes:

\[
\text{primitive coverage}
\rightarrow
\text{cards covered}
\]

rather than:

\[
\text{Card 1}
\rightarrow
\text{Card 2}
\rightarrow
\text{Card 3}.
\]

That will expose whether an abstraction is actually reusable.

For example, once you implement `DelayedEffect`, you may suddenly support “dies after two turns,” “attack after five moves,” “stun in three turns,” and several status-duration mechanics at once.

### The simulator should ultimately have three layers

The clean separation I would use is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Card data}
\rightarrow
\text{Rules/event engine}
\rightarrow
\text{Probability executor}
}
\]

The card layer says **what** happens.

The rules engine says **when and how effects interact**.

The probability executor decides whether to sample, branch exactly, merge branches, or prune.

That third separation is particularly important for your later transformer training because the neural system never needs to know how the battle was evaluated. It just receives:

\[
(\text{Team A},\text{Team B})
\rightarrow
P(\text{A wins}).
\]



::chatgpt-content-reference{index="0" is_streaming="false"}



The architectural decision I'd make **before writing the first card** is the event model and the immutable-definition/mutable-instance split. If those are right, the weirdest cards in your set mostly become combinations of existing pieces instead of reasons to restructure the simulator.

content.text: so the padding is mostly for the GPU

items.text:
Yes. Padding is mostly a **batching/parallelism convenience** for GPUs.

GPUs like dense rectangular tensors, so instead of processing descriptions with lengths

\[
6,\ 11,\ 19,\ 8,\ldots
\]

individually, you pack them into something like

\[
B\times L_{\max}
\]

where every sequence has the same length. Shorter ones get `PAD` tokens so the whole batch can be processed with large matrix operations.

Conceptually, the model should ignore those padded positions through masking, so they’re not really part of the description semantics.

There is a tradeoff though: padding wastes compute. If your longest description is 32 tokens but many descriptions are around 10 tokens, then a lot of attention work is being spent on masked positions.

You can reduce that with **length bucketing**. For example, batch descriptions of lengths 1–8 together, 9–16 together, 17–24 together, and so on. Then each batch pads only to its own local maximum.

For your corpus, though, 32 tokens is tiny, so the wasted compute is probably negligible. At \(d=128\) and only 2 layers, I’d favor the simpler fixed-width 32-token representation unless you’re processing enormous numbers of descriptions repeatedly.

And once the description vectors are precomputed, padding cost disappears from normal self-play anyway.

content.text: How do I deal with all the 0 tokens

items.text:
Treat `0` as **padding only**, not as a real vocabulary token.

For each description, suppose the stored row is:

```text
34, 1, 29, 7, 44, 31, 0, 0, 0, ...
```

The actual sequence is only:

```text
34, 1, 29, 7, 44, 31
```

Then at runtime construct:

```text
<BOS> 34 1 29 7 44 31 <CARD> <PAD> <PAD> ...
```

The important part is the attention mask. Every `<PAD>` position should be inaccessible:

\[
M_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{valid causal attention}\\
-\infty & \text{padding or future position}.
\end{cases}
\]

So the CARD token can attend to:

\[
\text{BOS + every real description token + itself}
\]

but never to the zeros.

For a causal transformer, conceptually the mask for

```text
BOS A B C CARD PAD PAD
```

looks like:

```text
        BOS A B C CARD PAD PAD
BOS      ✓
A        ✓  ✓
B        ✓  ✓ ✓
C        ✓  ✓ ✓ ✓
CARD     ✓  ✓ ✓ ✓  ✓
PAD      ×  × × ×  ×   ×
PAD      ×  × × ×  ×   ×   ×
```

The exact padding rows don't really matter if you never use their outputs, but masking their keys is important.

I would reserve:

\[
\boxed{\text{ID }0=\text{PAD}}
\]

and keep your actual vocabulary as IDs \(1\ldots439\). Then special tokens can follow, for example:

```text
0   PAD
1-439 vocabulary
440 BOS
441 CARD
```

You don't need a meaningful embedding for ID 0. The cleanest choice is:

\[
E_{\text{PAD}}=\mathbf 0
\]

and either keep that row permanently zero or use a framework's `padding_idx=0`, which normally prevents it from being trained.

One subtle point: **don't leave `<CARD>` after all 32 padded positions**.

Bad:

```text
BOS words... PAD PAD PAD ... PAD CARD
```

because then CARD always occupies the same final position but has dozens of meaningless locations between it and the description.

Better:

```text
BOS words... CARD PAD PAD PAD...
```

So if a description has \(n\) tokens,

\[
\operatorname{pos}(\text{CARD})=n+1
\]

after BOS.

That also means your learned positional embeddings naturally encode description length.

If you're doing next-token training at all, zeros also need to be excluded from the loss:

\[
L
=
-\sum_{t:\,x_t\neq\text{PAD}}
\log P(x_{t+1}|x_{\le t}).
\]

Otherwise the model will spend a huge fraction of its training effort learning:

> PAD predicts PAD predicts PAD predicts PAD.

For your current plan, where empirical game gradients are more important than LM pretraining, this is even simpler: just take the final `<CARD>` representation and completely ignore all outputs corresponding to padding.

So the zeros in the CSV are basically **storage placeholders**. Architecturally, the transformer should behave almost as though they were never there.

content.text: The small transformer can use sinsoidal P.E. but since the dimension is so tiny learned P.E. might perform better with almost no costs

items.text:
Yes. For the **small description transformer**, I’d favor learned absolute positional embeddings.

With \(d=128\) and only ~32 description positions, the cost is negligible:

\[
32\times128=4{,}096
\]

parameters—or about **4.3k** if you reserve a few extra positions for `<BOS>` and `<CARD>`. Against a ~460k description model, that's under 1%.

More importantly, your context has all the properties that favor learned PE:

\[
\boxed{\text{short}+\text{fixed maximum length}+\text{highly regular grammar}}
\]

There is essentially no need for sinusoidal PE's main advantage—generalizing to sequence lengths never encountered during training.

Learned PE can specialize to the peculiar structure of your canonical descriptions. For example, earlier positions may disproportionately contain triggers:

```text
on entry ...
on death ...
each turn ...
50 % chance ...
```

while later positions more often contain targets, durations, secondary clauses, and conditions. The positional vectors can exploit those corpus-specific regularities.

So each input is simply

\[
x_i=e_{\text{token}_i}+p_i,
\qquad p_i\in\mathbb R^{128}.
\]

### One thing I'd do carefully

Don't let padding determine the apparent location of `<CARD>`.

For:

```text
on entry attack enemy <CARD>
```

the CARD token should immediately follow the last real description token, not sit permanently at position 33 after 20+ padding tokens.

So internally you'd have something like:

```text
<BOS> on entry attack enemy <CARD> <PAD> <PAD> ...
```

and mask all padding.

Then `<CARD>` gets a position that represents the actual description length. That is useful information in itself.

Your 32-column stored matrix can still stay rectangular; just insert the special tokens at runtime before masking/padding.

### Learned PE might actually aid the mechanics parser

Because this isn't ordinary prose, word order has unusually strong semantic importance:

```text
gain 50 % damage after attacking
```

versus

```text
after gaining 50 % damage attack
```

and:

```text
on death heal next ally
```

versus

```text
heal on next ally death
```

Even if both use nearly identical vocabulary, their logic differs.

A learned absolute PE gives your two-layer model another easy way to encode these relationships rather than requiring the attention weights to infer all relative structure from scratch.

For the **big transformer**, learned PE is an even clearer choice because every position has explicit strategic meaning—ally support, ally slot 1, ally slot 2, enemy support, enemy slot 1, etc.

So I'd probably use learned absolute PE for **both**, for different reasons:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{small:} & \text{learn canonical rule syntax}\\
\text{big:} & \text{learn exact strategic slot semantics}.
\end{array}
\]

At these context lengths, sinusoidal encoding mostly saves a few thousand parameters you don't need to save.

content.text: I would add it directly to the 768-d card embeddings

items.text:
That’s cleaner.

If the strategic card vector is already

\[
c_i \in \mathbb R^{768},
\]

then just add a learned pack embedding of the same width:

\[
\boxed{
c_i' = c_i + e_{\text{pack}(i)}
}
\]

before the card enters the big transformer.

That treats pack identity exactly like a **metadata bias on strategic meaning** rather than something the description encoder has to interpret.

It also keeps the decomposition very clean:

\[
\text{description}
\rightarrow
128\text{-D semantic vector}
\rightarrow
768\text{-D strategic projection}
\]

then

\[
+\,768\text{-D pack embedding}
\]

then

\[
\text{big transformer}.
\]

Because pack identity is only a weak prior, I would initialize the pack embeddings with a relatively small scale so they do not dominate the projected card vectors initially. For example, if the card-vector RMS is around 1, initialize pack embeddings with something like RMS \(0.02\)–\(0.1\) and let training decide how much they should grow.

You can also regularize them lightly:

\[
L_{\text{pack}}=\lambda\|e_{\text{pack}}\|^2
\]

so the model uses pack identity only when it actually improves prediction.

A useful diagnostic would be the norm ratio

\[
r=
\frac{\|e_{\text{pack}}\|}
{\|c_i\|}.
\]

If \(r\) stays small, pack acts as intended: a weak era/design prior. If it grows toward 1 or above, the model may be leaning too heavily on pack identity.

And because it is additive, precomputation remains simple. Once both the strategic projection and pack embeddings are frozen:

\[
\tilde c_i
=
c_i+e_{\text{pack}(i)}
\]

can itself be cached.

So runtime still reduces to:

\[
\text{card ID}
\rightarrow
\tilde c_i
\rightarrow
\text{big transformer}.
\]

That’s probably better than concatenating pack metadata and forcing another projection layer to learn how to combine it.

content.text: There is also an optional embedding of card packs, it describes a broad set of cards that belong to an era of card development but their abilities aren't that related.

items.text:
Yes. I’d treat pack identity as **contextual metadata, not semantic mechanics**.

Because packs correspond to eras of card development, the embedding may still encode useful broad priors such as:

\[
\text{typical stat scale},\quad
\text{power creep},\quad
\text{mechanic complexity},\quad
\text{balance philosophy},\quad
\text{common interaction patterns}.
\]

But since cards within a pack are not necessarily mechanically related, I would **not add the pack embedding directly into the 128-D description token representation**. That risks making linguistic similarity partly mean “released together.”

A cleaner arrangement is:

\[
h_{\text{desc}}\in\mathbb R^{128}
\]

\[
e_{\text{pack}}\in\mathbb R^{8\text{–}32}
\]

then

\[
[h_{\text{desc}};e_{\text{pack}}]
\rightarrow
\text{strategic projection}
\rightarrow
c\in\mathbb R^{768}.
\]

For example:

\[
128+16=144
\rightarrow
384
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{GELU}}
768.
\]

That lets the projection decide whether pack information matters for a particular strategic feature without contaminating the language encoder itself.

I would keep the pack embedding **small**, probably around 8–16 dimensions initially. A 128-D pack embedding would be excessive because pack identity contains much less information than the description.

There is also a useful interpretation:

\[
h_{\text{desc}}
=
\text{“What does this card do?”}
\]

\[
e_{\text{pack}}
=
\text{“What design environment did this card come from?”}
\]

\[
c_{\text{strategic}}
=
\text{“What does that combination imply in the game?”}
\]

That division is quite clean.

The main danger is shortcut learning. Suppose newer packs are generally stronger. The model might discover:

\[
\text{newer pack}\Rightarrow\text{higher win probability}
\]

and underuse the actual description.

You can defend against that with **pack dropout** during training. Occasionally replace

\[
e_{\text{pack}}
\]

with a learned `<UNKNOWN_PACK>` embedding or zero vector. Then the network has to remain competent from mechanics alone.

Something like 10–30% pack dropout would be worth testing.

It also gives you a natural way to handle future packs:

\[
e_{\text{new pack}}=\text{UNKNOWN}
\]

until enough self-play has occurred to learn that pack's embedding.

Interestingly, you could also impose a weak temporal structure if the packs genuinely form chronological eras. Instead of treating every pack as an unrelated categorical ID, use

\[
e_{\text{pack}}
=
e_{\text{categorical}}
+
f(\text{release order}),
\]

but I wouldn't start there. Let the categorical embeddings reveal whether an era structure emerges by themselves.

And because there are probably relatively few packs, the parameter cost is almost nothing. Even:

\[
100\text{ packs}\times16
=
1600
\]

parameters.

So I'd absolutely include it as an **optional weak prior**, but place it immediately before the strategic projection rather than inside the linguistic transformer. That preserves the very useful distinction between **card meaning** and **historical/design context**.

content.text: is searching the classes faster than searching the cards for its corresponding bits

items.text:
Yes—if the number of classes is much smaller than the number of cards, **searching class membership is usually cheaper than searching a card-sized bitmap**.

Suppose you eventually have:

\[
N=2000\text{ cards},\qquad C=40\text{ classes}.
\]

If every card carries a 2000-bit relation bitmap, checking relationships means manipulating/searching a structure sized around \(N\).

But if a card instead stores its class memberships, you only deal with \(C\), or better, just the few classes actually attached to that card.

For example:

```text
Card 417:
[Dragon, Fire, RNG]
```

could simply store:

```text
[7, 12, 31]
```

Then testing

```text
is Dragon?
```

is only a search through perhaps 2–5 IDs:

\[
O(k),\qquad k\ll C\ll N.
\]

Even better, if \(C\) stays below 64, give each card one **64-bit class mask**:

\[
M_{\text{card}}
\]

and each class gets one bit.

Then:

\[
\text{is Dragon}
=
(M_{\text{card}}\;\&\;M_{\text{Dragon}})\neq0.
\]

That's effectively constant time.

So something like:

```text
bit 0 = Dragon
bit 1 = Undead
bit 2 = RNG
bit 3 = Bird
bit 4 = Friendship
...
```

lets one machine integer describe dozens of reusable card classes.

### For rare card-specific relationships

Don't put those into the class mask.

You could have:

```text
classes = 64-bit mask
specific_relations = [(Piccolo, SWAP_SYNERGY)]
```

Then the normal path is extremely cheap:

\[
\boxed{\text{class mask check}}
\]

and only the rare exceptional effects invoke a sparse card-ID lookup.

That gives you roughly:

\[
\text{frequent reusable mechanics}
\rightarrow
\text{bit mask}
\]

\[
\text{rare card-specific mechanics}
\rightarrow
\text{sparse relation list}.
\]

One nuance: if by "searching the cards for its corresponding bits" you mean a packed bitset over all cards, bitsets themselves are very fast. A 2000-card bitmap is only

\[
2000/64\approx32
\]

64-bit words. So intersection operations over whole sets can be efficient.

But for the common question

> "What properties/classes does this particular card have?"

a per-card class mask is much faster and much smaller.

For your model I'd probably use **both directions** where useful:

\[
\text{card}\rightarrow\text{class mask}
\]

for runtime checks, and optionally

\[
\text{class}\rightarrow\text{card bitset}
\]

for operations like "find every Dragon card."

That way neither operation requires scanning the entire card vocabulary.
